lecture_title: 1.1 - What is State and Why It's Hard
text: Hey everyone, and welcome to Build a State Management Library. Over the next twenty-four lectures we're going to build, from absolutely nothing, something that looks a lot like Zustand or a small Redux. Before we write a single line, I want us to agree on a word that gets thrown around constantly, and that's state. So what is state? The simplest definition I know is this: state is the data your program has to remember between two moments in time. The user added a shirt to their cart, and ten seconds later, when they click checkout, the program still has to know about that shirt. That memory is state. Everything else, the buttons, the layout, the colors, is just a picture drawn from it.

lecture_title: 1.1 - What is State and Why It's Hard
text: Now, why is it hard? Because state is shared and state changes. If one variable lived in one function and only that function touched it, we'd have no problem at all. But a cart total shows up in the header, in the checkout page, and in a small popup. Three places read it, and two or three places can write it. The moment you have many readers and many writers, you get questions. Who changed this value? When did it change? Did every reader notice? And that last question is the real killer, because a reader that missed an update shows the user a lie. Header says two items, checkout page says three. Okay, so keep that picture in your head.

lecture_title: 1.1 - What is State and Why It's Hard
text: Let me make it concrete with the app we'll use for this whole course, which is a shopping cart. Open a plain file called cart.js and I'll write `let cart = { items: [], total: 0 }`. Then a function `addItem(item)` that pushes onto `cart.items` and adds the price to `cart.total`. That works. Now I render a header that prints `cart.items.length`. I call addItem, and the header does nothing, because nothing told it to re-render. JavaScript has no idea that a variable changed. Plain objects don't announce anything. You'll notice that this single fact is the root of almost every problem in this course.

lecture_title: 1.1 - What is State and Why It's Hard
text: So you patch it. After every addItem call you manually call `renderHeader()`. Then you add a checkout page and have to remember `renderCheckout()` too. Then a teammate writes `cart.items.pop()` somewhere in a file you've never opened, and forgets to re-render anything. Now your UI is out of sync and nobody can tell where it happened. There are really three separate problems hiding here. One, how do we detect a change. Two, how do we tell everyone who cares. And three, how do we keep changes happening in a controlled, predictable place so that we can debug them. A state library is the answer to those three.

lecture_title: 1.1 - What is State and Why It's Hard
text: Let me add a fourth problem that shows up as apps grow, which is derived data. The cart total isn't really independent state, is it? It's just the sum of the item prices. If you store it separately, you now have two things that must always agree, and sooner or later they won't. Good libraries let you describe the derived value once and keep it fresh automatically. So here's our map for the course. Detect changes with Proxy, store and broadcast them, derive values lazily, control changes with actions, wrap everything in middleware, and finally record history so we can undo. In the next lecture, we'll see how the real libraries do it.

lecture_title: 1.2 - How Redux, Zustand, Pinia Work Under the Hood
text: In the last lecture we named the problems: detecting changes, notifying readers, and keeping writes predictable. In this lecture I want to look at how three real libraries answer those problems, because each of them made a different bet, and our library will borrow the best parts. We'll look at Redux, Zustand, and Pinia. I'm not going to open their source code line by line, I'm going to describe the core idea of each one, and I promise the idea is far smaller than you'd expect. Most of these libraries, at their heart, are a few dozen lines wrapped in a lot of ergonomics and documentation.

lecture_title: 1.2 - How Redux, Zustand, Pinia Work Under the Hood
text: Start with Redux. Redux says: keep all your state in one object, and never mutate it. The only way to change it is to dispatch an action, which is just a plain object like `{ type: 'cart/addItem', payload: item }`. A function called a reducer takes the old state and the action and returns a brand new state. Then the store calls every subscriber. Notice what Redux does not do: it doesn't detect changes at all. It doesn't need to, because the only door to change is dispatch, so it already knows when something happened. The price is boilerplate, since you write actions and reducers for everything.

lecture_title: 1.2 - How Redux, Zustand, Pinia Work Under the Hood
text: Zustand takes that idea and removes the ceremony. You call `create` with a function that receives `set` and `get`, and returns your state plus your functions. Under the hood a Zustand store is a closure holding a state variable and a Set of listeners. `setState` merges a partial object into the state, creating a new object with `Object.assign`, and then loops over the listeners. `subscribe` adds a listener and returns a function that removes it. That's genuinely most of it. React hooks on top just subscribe in an effect and re-render on change. Remember this shape, because it's exactly what we build in chapter three.

lecture_title: 1.2 - How Redux, Zustand, Pinia Work Under the Hood
text: Pinia, and Vue's reactivity before it, made the opposite bet. There you just mutate the state directly, `cart.items.push(item)`, and it works. How? Vue wraps your object in a JavaScript Proxy. A Proxy lets the library intercept every property read and every property write. On a read, it quietly records which piece of code is reading. On a write, it looks up who read that property and re-runs them. So Vue detects changes automatically, with no dispatch and no reducer. The tradeoff is that there's more magic, and state changes are harder to trace through a single choke point.

lecture_title: 1.2 - How Redux, Zustand, Pinia Work Under the Hood
text: So here's the interesting design question, and it's the one we'll answer. Can we get both? Zustand's simple store with subscribe, plus Pinia's automatic tracking with Proxy, plus Redux's discipline of controlled updates and replayable history. I think we can, and we'll do it in layers so each lecture adds one idea. Let me summarize the three bets in one line each. Redux: immutable updates through one door. Zustand: a tiny closure with listeners. Pinia: Proxy-based tracking. In the next lecture, I'll show you exactly what we're building and the folder layout, okay?

Alright, this is the last lecture of the first chapter, and it's a planning one. I want you to see the finish line before we start running, because the lectures after this are going to feel like small separate pieces, and I'd like you to know where each piece plugs in. The library is called statekit. It's plain JavaScript, ES modules, no build step, no dependencies. We'll test it with a small shopping cart app, so every concept gets used on something real rather than on abstract counters. By the end, statekit will do about six things, and I'll walk through them quickly now.

Piece one is reactivity, in a file called reactive.js. It exports a function `reactive(target, onChange)` that wraps an object in a Proxy and calls `onChange` whenever someone writes to it. Piece two is the core store, in store.js, exporting `createStore`. That gives us `getState`, `setState`, and `subscribe`. Piece three, computed.js, exports `computed(getter)`, so a value like `cartTotal` is derived from the items and cached. If any of this sounds abstract, don't worry, each one will take a whole lecture and we'll see it work in the browser console before moving on.

Piece four is actions. Instead of letting code scribble on the state from anywhere, we define named functions like `addItem` and `removeItem` and `checkout` inside the store. Some are async, and that's where optimistic updates and rollback come in, because a cart that calls a server needs to handle the server saying no. Piece five is middleware. That's a way to wrap `setState` so we can build a logger plugin in logger.js and a persistence plugin in persist.js that saves the cart to localStorage. Piece six, history.js, records snapshots so we get undo, redo, and a mini devtools.

Here's the folder layout. A folder called statekit with src inside it, and in src, reactive.js, store.js, computed.js, middleware.js, logger.js, persist.js, and history.js. Beside it, a folder called demo with index.html and cart-app.js, which is the shopping cart that exercises everything. I'd like you to create those now, empty files are fine. We'll work in modern browsers or Node, whichever you prefer, and I'll mostly use the browser console because seeing a header update live is a lot more satisfying than reading test output, though we'll do some of that too.

One last thing about how I'd like you to learn this. Please don't copy my code line for line. After each lecture, close the video and try to rebuild that file from memory. You'll get stuck, and the stuck place is exactly the spot you didn't fully understand. Also, notice the order we're building things in: each layer depends only on the layers before it. Reactivity knows nothing about stores, and the store knows nothing about middleware. That discipline is why the library stays small. Okay. In the next lecture we start with the foundation, JavaScript's Proxy, and we'll intercept our first property read. Take a moment to pause the video here and sketch those seven files on paper, because the sketch will help you later.

Welcome to chapter two. We're going to build the thing that detects change, and the tool for that in modern JavaScript is the Proxy. A Proxy is an object that wraps another object, called the target, and a second object, called the handler, that decides what happens when someone touches the wrapper. You create one with `new Proxy(target, handler)`. Everything the outside world does to the proxy, reading a property, writing a property, checking `in`, deleting, goes through the handler's traps first. Let's open reactive.js and the browser console side by side and just play with it for a minute before we build anything.

I'll type `const target = { count: 0 }` and then `const proxy = new Proxy(target, {})`. Empty handler. Now `proxy.count` gives zero, and `proxy.count = 5` changes the target too. With no traps, a Proxy is completely transparent, it just forwards everything. That's an important thing to see, because it tells us a Proxy never copies your data. It stands in front of it. Now let's add a trap. In the handler I'll write `get(target, key) { console.log('read', key); return target[key]; }`. Reading `proxy.count` now prints read count, and returns the value.

Let me add the write trap. `set(target, key, value) { console.log('write', key, value); target[key] = value; return true; }`. And I want to point at that `return true`, because it matters. In strict mode, if a set trap returns a falsy value, JavaScript throws a TypeError saying the proxy refused the assignment. Modules are always strict, so forgetting `return true` is one of the most common bugs when people first write a Proxy. Now `proxy.count = 7` prints write count 7. See what we've got? We now have a hook that fires on every single mutation, and nobody had to call a function to make it happen.

That is the whole trick behind Vue's reactivity. Reading goes through the get trap, writing goes through the set trap, and our library can attach behavior to both. Think about our cart. If `cart.items` is behind a Proxy, then a teammate who writes `cart.total = 99` somewhere far away still triggers our hook. We no longer rely on people remembering to call render. There's one catch I want to flag now and solve in a couple of lectures: a Proxy only intercepts access to the object it wraps. Nested objects, like the array inside `cart.items`, are separate objects, so they escape.

Let me prove that catch quickly. I'll wrap `{ items: [] }` in a proxy that logs writes, and then call `proxy.items.push('shirt')`. Nothing logs for the push, because `proxy.items` returns the raw array, and the push happens on the raw array, not on a proxy. Only `proxy.items = []` would be seen. So deep reactivity needs the get trap to return a proxy for nested objects too. We'll do that in lecture 2.3. For now, remember three things: a Proxy wraps a target, traps run before the operation, and the set trap must return true. Next, we'll clean up our traps using the Reflect API.

In the last lecture our traps did `return target[key]` and `target[key] = value`, and it worked, so you might ask why we need anything else. The answer is Reflect, and I want to show you the bug that Reflect fixes, because it's subtle. Reflect is a built-in object whose methods mirror the proxy traps one to one. `Reflect.get`, `Reflect.set`, `Reflect.has`, `Reflect.deleteProperty`, and so on. Each one does the default operation the language would have done without the proxy. So inside a trap, calling the matching Reflect method means do the normal thing, and you add your own behavior around it.

Let's see the first benefit, which is the return value. `Reflect.set(target, key, value)` returns a boolean telling you whether the assignment succeeded. That's exactly what the set trap is supposed to return. So instead of writing `target[key] = value; return true;` we write `return Reflect.set(target, key, value, receiver)`. If the property was frozen or non-writable, Reflect returns false, and the proxy correctly reports failure. The manual version would have thrown inside the trap, or lied and said true. Using Reflect gives us the language's own semantics for free, which is what we want in a library other people will trust.

Now the subtle bug. See that fourth argument I passed, `receiver`? Both the get and set traps receive it as their last parameter, and it's the object the operation was started on, usually the proxy itself. Why does it matter? Imagine a getter on our state, something like `get doubled() { return this.count * 2 }`. If our get trap does `target[key]`, then inside that getter `this` is the raw target, not the proxy. So the read of `this.count` skips our trap and tracking never sees it. With `Reflect.get(target, key, receiver)`, `this` is the proxy, and the nested read is intercepted. That's a real bug in naive implementations.

Let me demo it. I'll define an object with `count: 1` and a getter `double` returning `this.count * 2`. First proxy uses `target[key]`, with a log in the trap. Reading `proxy.double` logs only double. The inner count read is invisible. Now I switch to `Reflect.get(target, key, receiver)`, and reading `proxy.double` logs double and then count. That's the difference between a reactive system that notices derived values and one that quietly doesn't. Remember this for chapter four, because our computed values depend on exactly this behavior. Okay, any questions so far? The rule of thumb is simple.

The rule of thumb: inside a trap, perform the default behavior using the matching Reflect method with the same arguments, including receiver, and put your custom logic before or after it. Also, there's a bonus. Reflect methods are functions, so you can use them where operators would be awkward, like `Reflect.has(obj, 'x')` instead of `'x' in obj`, and `Reflect.ownKeys` for symbols too. Now we have all the parts we need. A Proxy to intercept, Reflect to behave correctly. In the next lecture we combine them into a real reactive primitive that calls our callback on every write, including nested ones.

Okay, this is where the chapter pays off. We're going to write the real `reactive` function in src/reactive.js. The signature is `reactive(target, onChange)`. It returns a proxy, and any time a property is set, added, or deleted anywhere in that tree, it calls `onChange(path, value)`. I'll start with the shell: `export function reactive(target, onChange) { const handler = { get, set, deleteProperty }; return new Proxy(target, handler); }`. Then let's fill each trap in, starting with the set trap, since writes are what we care about most for the store we're building in the next chapter.

Set trap. `set(obj, key, value, receiver)`. First I read the old value with `const old = obj[key]`. Then `const ok = Reflect.set(obj, key, value, receiver)`. Then, and this is a check I want you to remember, `if (ok && old !== value) onChange(key, value)`. Why compare? If someone writes the same value again, nothing really changed, and notifying would cause pointless re-renders. Using `Object.is` would be even stricter about NaN and negative zero, so let me use that: `!Object.is(old, value)`. Finally `return ok`. That's a correct, minimal set trap, and I'd like you to type it yourself now.

Next, deleteProperty, because `delete cart.coupon` is a mutation too and we'd miss it otherwise. `deleteProperty(obj, key) { const had = Reflect.has(obj, key); const ok = Reflect.deleteProperty(obj, key); if (ok && had) onChange(key, undefined); return ok; }`. We only notify if the key existed, same reasoning as before. Now the big one, the get trap, which handles nesting. `get(obj, key, receiver) { const value = Reflect.get(obj, key, receiver); if (typeof value === 'object' && value !== null) return reactive(value, onChange); return value; }`. Now `proxy.items` returns a proxy, and `proxy.items.push` is intercepted.

But there's a performance trap hiding in that get. Every read of `proxy.items` creates a brand new proxy. Not only is that wasteful, it breaks identity: `proxy.items === proxy.items` would be false, which will confuse anyone comparing objects. The fix is a cache. At module level I'll write `const proxyCache = new WeakMap()`. In reactive, first `if (proxyCache.has(target)) return proxyCache.get(target)`, then create the proxy, then `proxyCache.set(target, proxy)`. A WeakMap holds its keys weakly, so when the original object is garbage collected, the cache entry disappears with it. No memory leak, and identity is now stable.

Let's test it in the console with our cart. `const cart = reactive({ items: [], total: 0 }, (k, v) => console.log('changed', k, v))`. Then `cart.total = 10` logs changed total 10. And `cart.items.push({ id: 1, price: 10 })` logs twice, once for the index key zero and once for length, because push really does perform two writes. That's accurate, but noisy, and we'll solve it with batching when we build the store. Also, assigning `cart.total = 10` again logs nothing. We have a working reactive primitive in about thirty lines. In chapter three, we wrap it in a store. Take a moment now to type that final version out yourself and run it in the console before we move on, okay?

Welcome to chapter three. We have a primitive that can say something changed. Now we need a home for state, a container that owns it, protects it, and lets other code listen. That container is the store, and we'll build it in src/store.js. Before typing, let me describe the architecture, because the design is what separates a toy from a library. A store has exactly four responsibilities. Hold the current state. Provide a way to read it. Provide a controlled way to change it. And let other code subscribe to changes. If a feature doesn't fit one of those four, it probably belongs in a layer on top, not in the core.

Where should the state live? The cleanest answer in JavaScript is a closure. We write `export function createStore(initialState) { let state = initialState; ... }` and return an object of functions that close over `state`. Nobody outside can touch the variable `state` directly, they can only go through the functions we return. This is the module pattern, and it's what Zustand does. Compare that with a class that stores `this.state`: anyone can write `store.state = something`. A closure gives us real privacy without needing private fields, and it makes the store trivially safe to pass around.

Second design decision: mutable or immutable updates? We have the reactive primitive from last chapter, so mutation is tempting. But think about what later chapters need. Time travel needs old versions of state to still exist. Subscribers want to compare previous and next state. React-style rendering wants to check by reference whether something changed. All of that is easy if every update produces a new state object and leaves the old one alone, and miserable if we mutate in place. So the store's public updates are immutable: `setState` makes a new object. We'll use the reactive proxy for a different purpose, which I'll come back to.

Third decision: what's a listener, and how do we store them? A listener is just a function. We keep them in a `Set`, declared as `const listeners = new Set()` inside the closure. Why a Set rather than an array? Adding the same function twice shouldn't register it twice, and removing one is a constant-time `listeners.delete(fn)` rather than searching and splicing. Sets also iterate in insertion order, so listeners are called in the order they subscribed, which is a predictable behavior to document. Subscribing returns an unsubscribe function, so callers never need to hold a reference to the store to stop listening.

So the skeleton is: a closure with `state` and `listeners`, and three returned functions, `getState`, `setState`, and `subscribe`. Let me write the empty skeleton now so we have a target for the next two lectures. `export function createStore(initialState) { let state = initialState; const listeners = new Set(); const getState = () => state; const setState = () => {}; const subscribe = () => {}; return { getState, setState, subscribe }; }`. Notice that I'm returning a plain object of functions, not a class. In the next lecture we fill in subscriptions, and in the one after, the full API in action.

Let's fill in subscribe, since that's the mechanism that actually tells the rest of the world something changed. In store.js, `const subscribe = (listener) => { listeners.add(listener); return () => listeners.delete(listener); };`. Two lines. The first registers the function. The second returns an unsubscribe function, and that's the part people forget to think about. Every subscription is a potential memory leak, because the store holds a reference to your listener for as long as it's registered. In a UI, a component that disappears but never unsubscribes keeps being called forever. Returning the cleanup function makes the correct usage the easy usage.

Now, what does a listener receive? In the first version, we'd just call it with nothing, and the listener would call `getState()` itself. That works, but it forces each listener to ask. A better contract is to pass both the new state and the previous state: `listener(state, prevState)`. That's what Zustand does, and it's powerful. A listener can compare `state.items !== prevState.items` and skip work when the part it cares about hasn't changed. We'll lean on that a lot. So whatever notifies must hold on to the previous value before it replaces it. Keep that in mind for setState, which we write next.

Here's a question that trips people up. What happens if a listener unsubscribes itself, or subscribes a new listener, while we're in the middle of looping over the Set? Iterating a Set while modifying it is legal in JavaScript, but the behavior can surprise you. A listener added during iteration will be visited in that same loop, which might fire it for a change that happened before it subscribed. Deleted entries not yet visited are skipped. To keep things predictable, we'll copy first: `[...listeners].forEach(l => l(state, prevState))`. Now the set of listeners is frozen for that notification round.

And errors. If one listener throws, the forEach stops and every listener after it never hears about the change. That's a nasty bug, because the failing code could be in some analytics plugin and the thing that breaks is your header. For now, I'll leave it as is, because I want to keep the core small and obvious, and note in a comment that a production version might catch per listener. Let me show you the whole thing working. Create a store, call `store.subscribe(s => console.log('got', s))`, and keep the returned function in a variable called `unsub`. We can't change state yet, since setState isn't written.

That's the next lecture, but let me finish by setting up what we want to see. After we write setState, we'll subscribe two listeners, one logging the cart count and one logging the total. We'll call setState, and both fire. Then we'll call `unsub()` on the first one, call setState again, and only the second fires. That sequence is the entire contract of subscriptions: register, receive new and previous state, unregister. If you can explain why we return a function from subscribe and why we copy the listeners before looping, you've really understood this lecture. See you in 3.3.

Time to finish the store. We have subscribe from last lecture, and the empty getState. getState is simply `() => state`. Nothing clever, and that's the point, it returns the exact current object, not a copy, so reads are free. Now setState. Let me think about its signature before typing. I want to support two forms. A partial object, like `setState({ total: 20 })`, which merges into the existing state. And an updater function, like `setState(s => ({ total: s.total + 5 }))`, which receives the current state and returns a partial. The function form matters because it avoids stale reads when several updates happen in a row.

Here's the code. `const setState = (partial) => { const next = typeof partial === 'function' ? partial(state) : partial; if (Object.is(next, state)) return; const prevState = state; state = Object.assign({}, state, next); [...listeners].forEach(l => l(state, prevState)); };`. Let's walk through it. We resolve the function form. If the updater returned the very same state object, we bail out, nothing changed. Otherwise we remember the previous state, build a brand new object with `Object.assign({}, state, next)`, so the old one is untouched, and notify everyone with new and previous.

Let me show why the new object matters. In the console, `const store = createStore({ items: [], total: 0 })`. `const before = store.getState()`. Then `store.setState({ total: 10 })`. Now `const after = store.getState()`, and `before === after` is false, while `before.total` is still zero and `after.total` is ten. The old snapshot is intact. That immutability, which cost us one `Object.assign`, is what makes undo possible later in chapter seven. One warning: this merge is shallow. If you set `{ items: [...] }` you replace the whole items array. That's the same tradeoff Zustand makes, and it keeps updates predictable.

Now connect it to the cart. `store.subscribe((s, prev) => console.log('items', prev.items.length, '->', s.items.length))`. Then `store.setState(s => ({ items: [...s.items, { id: 1, name: 'Shirt', price: 20 }] }))`. We see items 0 to 1. Notice I created a new array with the spread instead of calling push, because pushing would mutate the old state and the previous and next items would be the same array. I want that to become a habit. Whenever you update, create new containers along the path. Okay, what about the reactive proxy from chapter two? Let's connect that now, because it gives us a nicer way to write updates.

Here's the connection. I'll add a method called `store.mutate(fn)`. It copies the state, wraps the copy in `reactive`, hands that proxy to the function so the user can write natural code like `draft.items.push(item)`, and when the proxy reports a change, we commit the copy through setState. That's essentially what Immer does, just much smaller and shallower. For this course I'll mostly use explicit setState, but keep reactive in your back pocket, since chapter four needs it for tracking. So we now have a complete core: getState, setState, subscribe. In chapter four, derived values.

Welcome to chapter four, computed state. Our store from chapter three holds `items` and a `total`, and I want to start by pointing at something uncomfortable about that. Is `total` really state? Think about it. If I know the items and their prices, I can always calculate the total. So the total is not an independent fact, it's a consequence of other facts. We call this derived state. And storing derived state next to the facts it comes from is one of the most common sources of bugs in real applications, so let's feel that bug before we fix it.

In the cart, I'll write `addItem` the way most people first would: `setState(s => ({ items: [...s.items, item], total: s.total + item.price }))`. Fine. Then a `removeItem` that filters the items and subtracts the price. Fine. Now we add coupons, and a quantity change, and a bulk clear. Every single function that touches items must remember to also fix the total. One teammate forgets in one place, and the header says forty dollars while the cart page says sixty. Nothing crashes. The two numbers just quietly disagree, and the bug report says the cart sometimes shows the wrong price.

The obvious fix is to not store it. Write a plain function: `const getTotal = (state) => state.items.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price * i.qty, 0)`. Now there's one source of truth, the items, and the total can never be stale, because it's computed every time you ask. That's actually a perfectly good solution for small apps, and I want to be fair to it. Selectors in Redux are exactly this, functions from state to a derived value. So what's wrong? Nothing, until the calculation gets expensive or the result needs to be an object that other code compares by reference.

Imagine a cart with two hundred items, and a derived value like `groupedByCategory`, which loops over everything and builds a new object. Called in the header, in the sidebar, and in the checkout summary, on every render, that's the same heavy work three times with identical inputs. Worse, each call returns a brand new object, so anything comparing by reference thinks it changed. What we want is a function that remembers its last result and only recomputes when something it actually read has changed. That's memoization, but with a twist: we want the library to figure out the dependencies automatically.

So here are the requirements for `computed`, in computed.js. One: you give it a getter function, like `() => cart.items.length`. Two: it caches the result. Three: it knows which state properties the getter read, without us declaring them. Four: when one of those properties changes, the cache is invalidated, but crucially, not recomputed until someone asks. That last piece is laziness. Number three is the hard part, the part that feels like magic, and it's built from a small trick with the Proxy get trap we wrote in chapter two. That's our next lecture.

Before we move on, check your understanding with a question. Why can't we just call the getter once, cache it forever, and be done? Right, because the inputs change. And why not just recompute on every state change? Because most changes are unrelated to this particular value, so we'd waste work. The sweet spot is to recompute only when a relevant input changes, and only when someone actually reads the result. To know which inputs are relevant, we need to record reads. Let's go build the recording machinery with a WeakMap, in the next lecture.

Here's the idea in one sentence: while a getter is running, every property it reads gets recorded as one of its dependencies. We already have the hook for that, the get trap from reactive.js. Today we add two helper functions to a new file, src/computed.js, called `track` and `trigger`. `track(target, key)` says the currently running function just read this property. `trigger(target, key)` says this property just changed, so go tell everyone who read it. The question is where to store that information, and the answer is a data structure with three levels of nesting, which looks scary but isn't.

Picture it as a table. Level one is a `WeakMap` whose keys are the raw target objects. For each object, level two is a `Map` from property name to level three, which is a `Set` of effects, where an effect is just a function that depends on that property. So `targetMap` maps an object to a map of keys to sets of effects. In code: `const targetMap = new WeakMap()`. Why a WeakMap at the top? Because the keys are your state objects, and if one is thrown away, we don't want our bookkeeping to keep it alive forever. The weak reference lets the garbage collector clean up automatically.

Now track. First we need to know who's reading right now, so I'll add a module variable: `let activeEffect = null`. Then `export function track(target, key) { if (!activeEffect) return; let depsMap = targetMap.get(target); if (!depsMap) targetMap.set(target, depsMap = new Map()); let dep = depsMap.get(key); if (!dep) depsMap.set(key, dep = new Set()); dep.add(activeEffect); }`. Read it slowly. If nobody is running, ignore the read. Otherwise find or create the map for this object, find or create the set for this key, and add the active effect. That's the whole recorder.

And trigger is the reverse lookup. `export function trigger(target, key) { const depsMap = targetMap.get(target); if (!depsMap) return; const dep = depsMap.get(key); if (!dep) return; [...dep].forEach(effect => effect.run ? effect.run() : effect()); }`. Again we copy the set before looping, same reason as with listeners, since effects may add themselves back while running. Now we wire these into reactive.js. In the get trap, right before returning, call `track(obj, key)`. In the set trap, after a successful change, call `trigger(obj, key)` in addition to the old `onChange`. Two small additions and the proxy now feeds the dependency table.

To make it testable, here's a tiny `effect` function: `export function effect(fn) { const run = () => { activeEffect = run; try { fn(); } finally { activeEffect = null; } }; run(); return run; }`. It sets itself as active, runs the function so reads get tracked, then clears it. Try it. `const state = reactive({ count: 1 }); effect(() => console.log('count is', state.count));` That logs count is 1 immediately. Then `state.count = 2` logs count is 2 on its own. We've built automatic dependency tracking. Nobody declared that the effect depends on count. It just read it.

One refinement I want to mention honestly. Our `activeEffect` is a single variable, so if an effect runs another effect inside it, the inner one overwrites the outer and the outer is left with no active effect when it resumes. Real libraries keep a stack, or save and restore the previous value. Let me do the simplest fix: inside run, write `const prev = activeEffect; activeEffect = run; try { fn(); } finally { activeEffect = prev; }`. Now nesting works. Okay. We can track and trigger. In the next lecture we use that to build computed itself, with caching and laziness.

Alright, we have an effect function that re-runs eagerly whenever its dependencies change. That's great for side effects like rendering, but it's the wrong behavior for a computed value. If three things change in a row, an eager recompute would run the heavy getter three times, even if nobody looked at the result in between. We want computed to be lazy. So in computed.js we'll build `computed(getter)` on a different foundation: instead of re-running on change, a change merely marks the value as dirty. The getter runs only when someone reads `.value` and the cache is dirty.

Here's the shape. `export function computed(getter) { let value; let dirty = true; const runner = () => { ... }; return { get value() { ... } }; }`. We need two flags of state, the cached `value` and a boolean `dirty`. The returned object has a getter named `value`, which is a nice use of the object getter syntax from earlier: reading `total.value` looks like reading a property, but it's running our code. Initially dirty is true, because we haven't computed anything yet. Let's write what happens inside that getter, since all the logic lives there.

Inside the value getter: `if (dirty) { value = runWithTracking(getter, markDirty); dirty = false; } track(self, 'value'); return value;`. Let me unpack it. If dirty, we recompute, but while recomputing, we want the reads inside the getter to be tracked, and we want the reaction to a change to be markDirty, not an immediate re-run. So I'll generalize effect to accept a scheduler. `effect(fn, { scheduler })`: when trigger finds an effect with a scheduler, it calls `scheduler()` instead of `run()`. That's the same trick Vue uses, and it's a two-line change in trigger.

So the computed creates its effect with `scheduler: () => { if (!dirty) { dirty = true; trigger(self, 'value'); } }`. Read that carefully. When a dependency changes, the scheduler fires. It flips dirty to true, and then triggers anyone who depended on this computed's value. That second step matters: a computed can be read by an effect, or by another computed, and they need to be told that their input is now stale. We use the computed object itself as the target and the string value as the key, so the same targetMap machinery handles computed-on-computed with no extra code.

Let's run it. `const cart = reactive({ items: [{ price: 10, qty: 2 }] })`. `const total = computed(() => { console.log('computing'); return cart.items.reduce((s, i) => s + i.price * i.qty, 0); })`. Nothing logs yet, because it's lazy. `total.value` logs computing and returns twenty. Again `total.value`, returns twenty, no log, cached. Now `cart.items[0].qty = 3`. Still no log, only dirty was set. `total.value` logs computing and returns thirty. One computation per change, and none when nobody asks. That is exactly the behavior we wanted.

A few honest notes. Our version doesn't clean up stale dependencies. If the getter reads `cart.coupon` only in some branches, an old dependency can linger and cause an extra dirty mark. That's harmless but wasteful, and production libraries clear and re-collect dependencies on each run. Also, we're not yet connected to the store from chapter three. In the next chapter we'll hook computed values onto store state, alongside actions. For now, make sure you can explain these three words in your own sentence: track, trigger, dirty. If you can, chapter four is done.

Welcome to chapter five, actions and mutations. So far, anything with a reference to the store can call `setState` with anything. That's powerful and also terrifying, because when the cart shows the wrong thing six weeks from now, you have to search the entire codebase for every place that calls setState. Redux's big insight was to make the set of possible changes explicit and named. Zustand does it more gently, by convention. We'll do the Zustand version: define actions, which are named functions, right next to the state, and have components call those instead of setState.

In store.js, I'll change the signature to `createStore(initialState, createActions)`. The second argument is optional and it's a function that receives `set` and `get`, and returns an object of action functions. So for our cart: `const cart = createStore({ items: [], total: 0 }, (set, get) => ({ addItem: (item) => set(s => ({ items: [...s.items, item] })), removeItem: (id) => set(s => ({ items: s.items.filter(i => i.id !== id) })), clear: () => set({ items: [] }) }))`. Notice there's no total there anymore, since we'll hang that off computed. Each action is one named, greppable, testable function.

Inside createStore, after we create setState and getState, we add `const actions = createActions ? createActions(setState, getState) : {}` and include `actions` in the object we return. Now usage is `cart.actions.addItem({ id: 1, name: 'Shirt', price: 20, qty: 1 })`. The function closes over `set` and `get`, so it needs no reference to the store object, which avoids a nasty circular reference between the store and its own actions. And `get` is useful, because an action can read the current state to decide what to do, for example refusing to add a fifth discount code.

Let me add something that makes mutations explicit in a stricter way, optional but instructive. I'll add a name to each change: `set(partial, 'cart/addItem')`. The second argument is just a label, stored and passed to listeners as a third parameter, `listener(state, prevState, actionName)`. It costs us nothing now, and it's what lets the logger plugin and the time-travel devtools show a readable list of what happened, rather than anonymous state diffs. Redux makes you write the type string anyway, so we're getting the same traceability with less ceremony. Remember that label, we'll use it heavily in chapters six and seven.

There's also a question of validation. Because every change goes through an action, that's the one place to enforce rules. For `addItem`, I can check `if (item.price < 0) throw new Error('Price cannot be negative')`. For `removeItem`, silently do nothing if the id isn't present rather than creating a new state object for no reason. And by returning early without calling set, no listeners fire. If you've ever debugged a component that re-rendered on every click for no visible reason, you know how valuable it is that no-op actions produce no notification.

To wrap up, here's what we've established. State is read through getState and computed values. State is changed only through actions. Actions are plain functions that call set with a partial or an updater. Nothing stops a determined developer from calling setState directly, and that's deliberate, because JavaScript has no way to truly forbid it. The discipline is convention plus tooling. In the next lecture we deal with the case where an action needs to talk to a server, and we want the UI to feel instant, using optimistic updates.

Real carts talk to servers. When you click add to cart, the browser sends a request, and the server answers a few hundred milliseconds later. If we wait for the answer before updating the screen, the interface feels sluggish. Optimistic updates fix that: we update the state immediately, assuming the request will succeed, and then reconcile when the real answer arrives. It's what makes apps like email clients feel instant. The cost is that we now owe the user a correction if the assumption was wrong. In this lecture we build the optimistic half, and in the next, the rollback half.

First, a fake server so we can test. In demo/api.js I'll write `export function saveItem(item) { return new Promise((resolve, reject) => setTimeout(() => Math.random() < 0.3 ? reject(new Error('Server said no')) : resolve({ ...item, serverId: Date.now() }), 500)); }`. Half a second of delay, and thirty percent of calls fail. That's rude but realistic. It gives us a controllable way to see both outcomes. Now back in our action factory, let's write `addItemAsync`. Because actions are plain functions, an async one is just an async function. The store doesn't need to know anything special about it, which is a lovely property of this design.

Here's the naive version, which waits: `addItemAsync: async (item) => { const saved = await saveItem(item); set(s => ({ items: [...s.items, saved] })); }`. The screen doesn't change for half a second. Now let's make it optimistic by reordering. `addItemAsync: async (item) => { const temp = { ...item, pending: true }; set(s => ({ items: [...s.items, temp] })); const saved = await saveItem(item); set(s => ({ items: s.items.map(i => i === temp ? saved : i) })); }`. The item appears immediately, marked pending, and when the server answers, we swap the temporary object for the real one.

A detail I want you to notice: I compare `i === temp` by reference, which is why we immutably created `temp` and kept a handle on it. If I had searched by id, and the user added two of the same product quickly, I'd have replaced the wrong one. In real apps, you'd give each optimistic item a client generated id, something like `crypto.randomUUID()`, and swap by that. The pending flag is useful too. The UI can show the row slightly greyed out, and disable the checkout button while any item is still pending. That's derived state, so a computed value, `hasPending`, is the right tool.

There's a subtle issue called a race. The user clicks add, then immediately clicks add again on the same item. Two requests are in flight. They might come back out of order. Because each response swaps its own temp object, we're safe for adds. But for something like setting a quantity, the older request returning last would overwrite the newer value. The standard defense is a request counter: store a sequence number with each call, and ignore a response if a newer one has already been started. We won't build that now, but I want you to know it exists.

So where are we? We have an action that updates the state instantly, with a temporary, pending-marked item, and swaps in the real one on success. What happens on failure? Right now, the promise rejects, our function throws after the await, and the temporary item stays in the cart forever, a ghost item that the server never knew about. That's the bug we're going to fix in the next lecture, with rollback. Before then, try it yourself: call addItemAsync a few times until one fails, and look at the stuck item.

Last lecture ended with a ghost item stuck in the cart after a failed request. Let's fix it. Rollback means: if the optimistic assumption turns out wrong, restore the state to what it was, or to what it should be now. There are two common strategies. The first is snapshot rollback: before the optimistic update, save the previous state, and on failure put it back. The second is inverse rollback: on failure, apply the opposite change, remove the temp item. Both are valid, and which one is right depends on what else might have changed while the request was in flight.

Let's write the snapshot version first because it's the simplest to reason about. `addItemAsync: async (item) => { const snapshot = get().items; const temp = { ...item, pending: true }; set(s => ({ items: [...s.items, temp] }), 'cart/addItem:optimistic'); try { const saved = await saveItem(item); set(s => ({ items: s.items.map(i => i === temp ? saved : i) }), 'cart/addItem:confirmed'); } catch (err) { set({ items: snapshot }, 'cart/addItem:rollback'); throw err; } }`. Notice the action labels. They'll make this sequence readable later in our logger.

Now let me tell you why snapshot rollback is dangerous. While our request was in flight, the user might have added a second item, successfully. When the first one fails, we restore the snapshot taken before either, and the second item vanishes, even though the server accepted it. That's data loss, and it's a classic optimistic update bug. Snapshot rollback is only safe when nothing else can change that slice of state during the request. So for a cart, where users click rapidly, we want the inverse approach instead. Let me show you what that looks like in code.

Inverse rollback: in the catch block, `set(s => ({ items: s.items.filter(i => i !== temp) }), 'cart/addItem:rollback')`. We remove only the temp item and leave everything else alone, using the same reference check as before. Now the second item survives. For removal, the inverse is to put the removed item back at its original index. That means capturing the index before removing. Slightly more bookkeeping, but each action knows exactly how to undo itself. I think of it as every optimistic action returning a tiny undo function, which we could even formalize as a helper called `optimistic`.

Let's formalize it, since we'll write this pattern repeatedly. `async function optimistic(set, apply, undo, request) { set(apply, 'optimistic'); try { return await request(); } catch (err) { set(undo, 'rollback'); throw err; } }`. Four inputs: how to apply the change, how to undo it, and the request to run. The helper handles ordering and rethrowing. Then `addItemAsync` shrinks to a single call. Rethrowing matters, by the way. The state is repaired, but the caller still needs to know it failed, so the UI can show a message like couldn't add that, please try again.

That wraps chapter five. Let's recap in a few sentences. Actions are named functions that call set. Async actions are just async functions. Optimistic updates apply a change immediately and mark it pending. Rollback should usually be inverse rather than snapshot, because other changes may have happened in the meantime. And the rollback must rethrow so the caller can react. In chapter six we move on to middleware, a way to wrap every one of these set calls with shared behavior, like logging and saving to localStorage, without touching any action code.

Welcome to chapter six. By now our store has a clear core, and we keep wanting to add behavior around it. We want to log every change in development. We want to save the cart to localStorage. We might want analytics later, or validation. We could bolt each of these into setState directly, but then setState becomes a tangle, and users can't opt in or out. Middleware is the answer you've seen in Express, Redux, and Koa. It's a function that wraps another function, can run code before and after, and decides whether to call it at all.

Let's define the shape precisely, because getting the shape right is ninety percent of the work. In our library, a middleware is a function that takes the next `setState` and returns a new `setState`. Written as arrows: `const middleware = (next) => (partial, label) => { ...; next(partial, label); ...; }`. The outer function receives whatever comes after it in the chain. The inner function has the same signature as setState itself, which is the key. Since it looks just like setState, wrapped or not, the rest of the system can't tell the difference, and middleware can stack indefinitely.

Now we apply them. In store.js, I'll add a third option: `createStore(initialState, createActions, middlewares = [])`. After defining the raw setState, we compose: `let dispatch = rawSetState; for (const mw of [...middlewares].reverse()) dispatch = mw(dispatch);`. Why reverse? Because we're wrapping from the inside out. The last middleware in the list wraps the raw function first, so the first in the list ends up outermost and runs first. That gives users the intuitive reading order: the array is the order things happen in. Then actions get `dispatch` as their `set`, not the raw one.

Let me write a trivial middleware so we can feel it. `const timestamp = (next) => (partial, label) => { console.log('before', Date.now()); next(partial, label); console.log('after', Date.now()); }`. Pass `[timestamp]` into createStore, call `cart.actions.addItem(...)`, and you see before, then the state change notifying listeners, then after. Notice that listeners run inside next, because notification is part of the raw setState. So code after `next` in a middleware runs after all subscribers have been told. That ordering is guaranteed and worth remembering, since persistence will depend on it.

Middleware can also block or transform. If a middleware never calls `next`, the update is dropped. That's how a validation plugin would reject bad changes. And if it calls `next` with a modified partial, it transforms them, like a plugin that stamps every update with `updatedAt`. One subtlety is function-form partials. The partial could be an updater function, and the middleware doesn't know the resulting state until it runs. To handle this, middlewares that need the result read `getState()` after calling next. We'll see that in the logger. Next lecture, the logger plugin, our first real middleware.

A quick comparison to close. Redux middleware has the shape `store => next => action`, with three levels, because it receives the store API first. Ours has two, since we use closures, so each plugin that needs state takes it as an argument to a factory function, like `logger({ collapsed: true })` returning the middleware. That factory pattern is how plugins accept configuration. So the full picture: a plugin is a function that returns a middleware, which is a function that takes next and returns a replacement setState. Let's go and write one.

Let's build our first real plugin, the logger. Open a new file, src/logger.js. What do we want to see? For every state change, the action label, the state before, the state after, and maybe the time it took. That's the output of Redux Logger, and it's the single most useful debugging tool I know. When something goes wrong in the cart, the log tells you the story. The challenge is that a middleware wraps setState, so it only sees the partial, not the state. To log before and after, we need access to getState. That's why our plugin is a factory.

So: `export function logger(options = {}) { return (getState) => (next) => (partial, label) => { ... } }`. Hmm, that's now three levels, so let me simplify instead. I'll change the contract slightly. Middlewares will receive a small API object as a second argument: `(next, api)` where `api` has `getState`. In createStore, the composition becomes `dispatch = mw(dispatch, { getState })`. The logger is then `export const logger = (options = {}) => (next, api) => (partial, label = 'anonymous') => { ... }`. Still two levels beyond the options. Make that small edit in store.js now, and I'll wait.

Inside the logger: `const prev = api.getState(); const start = performance.now(); next(partial, label); const nextState = api.getState(); const ms = (performance.now() - start).toFixed(2);`. Then output. `console.groupCollapsed('%c' + label + ' @ ' + new Date().toLocaleTimeString() + ' (' + ms + 'ms)', 'color: gray')`, then `console.log('prev state', prev)`, `console.log('next state', nextState)`, and `console.groupEnd()`. In the browser, that gives a collapsible group per change. I used `performance.now` rather than `Date.now` because it has sub-millisecond resolution, which matters for fast updates like these.

Let's use it: `createStore(initial, actions, [logger()])`. Call addItem and in the console we see a group named cart/addItem, expand it, and there are the previous and next states. With async, we get three groups in a row: optimistic, then confirmed or rollback, which is why we added those labels in chapter five. The sequence reads like a story. And you can see in one glance whether the rollback ran. If you've ever added console.log statements all over an app to understand a bug, you'll appreciate having this for free.

A few options make it production worthy. `collapsed`, a boolean, chooses between group and groupCollapsed. `filter`, a function receiving the label, lets you hide noisy actions like mouse move updates. `diff`, a boolean, logs only the changed keys, computed with a simple loop comparing prev and next. I'll add the filter now: `if (options.filter && !options.filter(label)) return next(partial, label);`. At the top of the inner function. Early return means we skip all the logging work, and the update still goes through. Always remember the middleware must call next on every path, or it silently blocks.

One more thing, which is guarding against production. A logger that dumps your whole cart state, possibly containing personal details, to the console, is not something you want shipped. The usual approach is `enabled: process.env.NODE_ENV !== 'production'`, defaulting to enabled in development. If disabled, the factory returns an identity middleware, `(next) => next`, which has zero overhead. That's a neat property of our design: a disabled plugin costs nothing. Next lecture, a more consequential plugin, one that writes to localStorage, and has a few traps of its own.

Our second plugin is persistence. A user fills their cart, refreshes the page, and the cart is gone. That's frustrating, so we'll save the state to localStorage and restore it on load. Create src/persist.js. The plugin has two jobs: hydrate, meaning read saved state at startup, and save, meaning write on changes. Hydration is the trickier one, because it happens before the store exists, or at least before any middleware runs, so a pure setState wrapper can't do it alone. Let's think about how to give plugins a chance to influence the initial state.

The simplest approach is to let the persist function wrap the initial state itself, not just the setState. `export function persist(key, options = {}) { const storage = options.storage || localStorage; return { hydrate(initial) { ... }, middleware: (next, api) => (partial, label) => { ... } }; }`. So a plugin can be an object with optional parts. In createStore, if a plugin has a hydrate function, we call `state = plugin.hydrate(state)` while creating, and if it has middleware, we compose it. It's a small extension of our design, and it's where middleware becomes plugin. Let's write hydrate now.

Hydrate: `hydrate(initial) { try { const raw = storage.getItem(key); if (!raw) return initial; return { ...initial, ...JSON.parse(raw) }; } catch { return initial; } }`. We wrap it in try and catch because stored data can be corrupted, the user could have edited it, or localStorage can throw if it's disabled, as in some private browsing modes. Falling back to the initial state is always safe. And we merge over initial, rather than replacing, so if a newer version of the app added a new field, it gets its default instead of being undefined. That tiny spread saves a lot of migrations.

Now the saving middleware: `(next, api) => (partial, label) => { next(partial, label); try { storage.setItem(key, JSON.stringify(api.getState())); } catch {} }`. We call next first, so we save the final state after subscribers have been notified. And again try and catch, since setItem throws when the quota is exceeded, roughly five megabytes in most browsers. One more important point: JSON can't hold functions, so our actions, which live in a separate object and not in state, are fine. Had we put functions inside state, they'd silently vanish. Another reason actions live beside state, not in it.

Performance next. Every keystroke in a form bound to the store would call JSON.stringify and write synchronously. localStorage is synchronous and can be slow. A standard fix is debouncing: wait until updates pause for, say, a hundred milliseconds before writing. `let timer; ... clearTimeout(timer); timer = setTimeout(save, options.delay ?? 100)`. Also, add a `partialize` option, a function that picks which fields to save, so we persist items but not transient values like pending flags or error messages. Persisting a pending flag would mean a ghost loading spinner after refresh.

There are two more production concerns I'll mention without coding. Versioning: store a version number alongside the data, and run a migration function when it changes, so old saved shapes don't crash a new app. And cross-tab sync: the browser fires a `storage` event in other tabs when one tab writes, so you can listen and call setState to keep tabs in agreement. That's chapter six done. We have a middleware pattern, a logger, and persistence. Chapter seven is the fun one. Using the fact that every state is an immutable snapshot, we'll build undo, redo, and a devtools-style time machine.

Welcome to chapter seven, time-travel debugging, which is the payoff for a decision we made way back in lecture 3.3. Remember that setState builds a new object with Object.assign and never touches the old one? Every state our cart has ever been in is a perfectly good snapshot, sitting in memory as long as someone holds a reference to it. Time travel is nothing more than holding on to those references in a list and putting an old one back when asked. No magic, no special proxies. Today we design the history structure, and next lecture we build undo and redo on top of it.

You might worry about memory. Isn't copying the whole state on every change expensive? Here's the good news, and it's called structural sharing. When we do `{ ...state, items: newItems }`, the new state object shares every untouched value with the old one by reference. If the cart has a huge catalog object that didn't change, both snapshots point at the same catalog in memory. Only the path to what changed is new. So storing a hundred snapshots costs roughly a hundred small objects plus the changed branches, not a hundred copies of everything. That's why immutability and history go together so naturally.

Now the data structure. There are two designs. One is a single array of snapshots with a pointer to the current index. The other is three pieces: a `past` array, the `present` state, and a `future` array. I prefer the second because the operations read like English. Undo means push the present onto future, and pop the last of past to become the present. Redo is the reverse. A brand new change means push the present onto past, set the new present, and clear the future, because once you branch off in a new direction, the old redo path no longer makes sense.

Let me sketch it in src/history.js. `export function withHistory(store, options = {}) { const limit = options.limit ?? 50; let past = []; let future = []; let travelling = false; ... }`. The limit is important. History grows without bound otherwise, and a long session would eat memory. When past exceeds the limit, we drop the oldest with `past.shift()`. The `travelling` boolean is a guard I'll explain properly next lecture, but the short version is that when we restore a snapshot, that restore itself is a state change, and we mustn't record it as new history.

How does history learn about changes? By subscribing, using the store API we built in chapter three. `store.subscribe((state, prev, label) => { if (travelling) return; past.push({ state: prev, label }); if (past.length > limit) past.shift(); future = []; })`. The listener receives the previous state, which is exactly what we wanted to save, and the label from chapter five, so each history entry knows which action produced the move away from it. That's why those labels were worth adding. Our history entries will say cart/addItem and cart/removeItem, not just a blob of data.

One design question: what about changes we don't want in history? Pending flags flipping during an optimistic update would make undo steps that look like nothing happened. A filter option helps: `options.filter?.(label)` returns false to skip recording. Also grouping, where several rapid changes should undo as one, like typing a coupon code. We won't implement grouping, but I want you to know that's where real undo systems get complicated. For now, we record every labelled change. In the next lecture, we write undo, redo, and a canUndo check.

Let's finish history.js with the three operations people actually want: undo, redo, and jump. First though, a small change in store.js. Our setState merges a partial into the old state, but restoring a snapshot needs to replace the state wholesale, otherwise a key that was added later would survive the undo. So I'll give setState an optional third argument, `replace`. If true, `state = next` instead of `Object.assign`. In code: `state = replace ? next : Object.assign({}, state, next)`. Everything else stays identical, including notifying listeners. That's the only core change time travel needs.

Now undo. `function undo() { if (!past.length) return; const entry = past.pop(); future.push({ state: store.getState(), label: entry.label }); travelling = true; store.setState(entry.state, '@@undo', true); travelling = false; }`. Walk through it. Guard on empty. Take the most recent past entry. Save the current state onto future so redo can come back. Set travelling to true, restore with replace, set it back to false. Because listeners run synchronously inside setState, our history subscriber sees travelling is true and ignores that notification. That is exactly why the flag exists.

Redo mirrors it. `function redo() { if (!future.length) return; const entry = future.pop(); past.push({ state: store.getState(), label: entry.label }); travelling = true; store.setState(entry.state, '@@redo', true); travelling = false; }`. If you compare undo and redo side by side, they're symmetric, a swap between two stacks. I'd encourage you to write redo yourself before looking at mine. Then `canUndo = () => past.length > 0` and `canRedo = () => future.length > 0`. Those drive the disabled state of undo and redo buttons in the cart UI, so users can't click something that does nothing.

Let's try it in the cart. `const history = withHistory(cart)`. Add a shirt, add a hat, add shoes. Three entries in past. `history.undo()`, and shoes disappear and the header updates, because the listeners fired with the restored state. Again, hat disappears. `history.redo()`, hat is back. Now add socks instead. The future is cleared, so redo does nothing, and the shoes are gone forever from the redo path. That's the standard behavior of every editor you've used, and we got it in about thirty lines because immutability did the heavy lifting.

Add jump too: `function jumpTo(index) { while (past.length > index) undo(); }` handles going backwards by repeated undo, and going forward uses redo similarly. It's inefficient for big jumps, but it's honest and obviously correct. A faster version would splice the stacks directly. Finally, return the API: `return { undo, redo, canUndo, canRedo, jumpTo, entries: () => past.map(p => p.label) }`. The entries list is what a devtools panel would render. Which brings us to the last lecture of the chapter, where we connect this all to the Redux DevTools browser extension.

One gotcha before we leave. Persistence from chapter six and history interact. If undo restores a state via setState, the persist middleware sees it and saves that, which is what you want, since the stored cart should match what's on screen. But the middleware order matters: history subscribes at the store level, so it's independent of the middleware chain. Another gotcha is async actions. If you undo while an optimistic request is in flight, the pending item vanishes, and when the server confirms, the swap finds nothing to replace. Our map-based swap simply does nothing, which is a graceful failure.

lecture_title: 7.3 - How Redux DevTools Works Under the Hood
text: You've probably used the Redux DevTools browser extension. It shows a list of actions on the left, the state tree on the right, and a slider you can drag to travel through time. It feels like a complicated product, but the way it talks to your app is surprisingly small. When the extension is installed, it puts one global on the page: `window.__REDUX_DEVTOOLS_EXTENSION__`. Your code checks whether that exists. If it does, you call `connect` on it, and you get back a connection object. Everything else is sending messages and receiving messages. And it works with any state container, not just Redux, which is why Zustand has a devtools middleware.

lecture_title: 7.3 - How Redux DevTools Works Under the Hood
text: Let's build ours as a plugin in src/devtools.js. `export function devtools(name = 'statekit') { return { connect(store) { const ext = window.__REDUX_DEVTOOLS_EXTENSION__; if (!ext) return; const conn = ext.connect({ name }); conn.init(store.getState()); ... } }; }`. The guard on `ext` matters, since most of your users won't have the extension, and the app must work without it. The `name` option labels this store in the extension's instance dropdown, handy when an app has several stores. And `conn.init` sends the starting state, which becomes the first entry in the timeline.

lecture_title: 7.3 - How Redux DevTools Works Under the Hood
text: Sending updates is one line, because we already have exactly what it wants. `store.subscribe((state, prev, label) => conn.send({ type: label || 'anonymous' }, state))`. The first argument is the action, an object that needs a `type` string. The second is the new state. The extension appends a row to its action list, and stores that snapshot. See how all the labels we added in earlier chapters now pay off? Without them, the extension's list would read anonymous, anonymous, anonymous, which is useless. Open the cart, click add, and the row cart/addItem appears in the panel, with a diff of the state.

lecture_title: 7.3 - How Redux DevTools Works Under the Hood
text: The reverse direction is how the slider works. When you drag it in the extension, it sends your page a message. We listen with `conn.subscribe(message => { ... })`. For time travel, the message looks like `{ type: 'DISPATCH', payload: { type: 'JUMP_TO_STATE' }, state: '...json string...' }`, and there's a similar `JUMP_TO_ACTION`. The state arrives as a JSON string, because the extension lives in a separate process and everything crosses as text. So we write `if (message.type === 'DISPATCH' && (message.payload.type === 'JUMP_TO_STATE' || message.payload.type === 'JUMP_TO_ACTION')) { store.setState(JSON.parse(message.state), '@@devtools', true); }`.

lecture_title: 7.3 - How Redux DevTools Works Under the Hood
text: Notice the extension keeps its own copy of every snapshot, so it isn't depending on our history stack at all. That means two things. First, when we apply a state from the devtools, our own history shouldn't record it, which we can handle with the same travelling idea, or by ignoring labels beginning with the at sign at sign. Second, serialization matters. The state goes through JSON, so Maps, Sets, functions, and class instances don't survive the trip. This is one more argument for keeping state as plain data, which is what we've done all along with our cart items.

lecture_title: 7.3 - How Redux DevTools Works Under the Hood
text: So the whole mystery is this: a global to detect, a connect call, an init, a send per change, and a subscribe for incoming jump messages. About thirty lines total. And now we've covered what time travel really is. Immutable snapshots, a list of them, and a way to put one back. Everything you saw in the extension demos, you could build. That ends chapter seven. In the last chapter, we compare what we built with Zustand itself, learn how to publish it as an npm package, and talk about what to explore next.

Welcome to our final chapter. Let's put statekit next to Zustand and see what we got right, what we simplified, and what real libraries do that we didn't. I'll be careful to speak about Zustand's design in general terms. Zustand's vanilla core is tiny, famously around fifty lines, and honestly if you compare it with our store.js, you'll recognize it. A closure holding state, a Set of listeners, `getState`, `setState`, and `subscribe`. The setState takes a partial or a function, checks with `Object.is` whether anything changed, merges with Object.assign, and notifies each listener with state and previous state. We made the same choices.

Where do we differ? First, replace. Zustand's setState also accepts a second argument, `replace`, which swaps the state entirely instead of merging. We added the same thing for time travel. Second, actions. In Zustand, your state creator is a function receiving set, get, and the api, and it returns state and actions together in one object. We separated them into a second argument. The Zustand approach is more compact, but it means functions live inside state, which is why its persist middleware has to deal with that, using a `partialize` option. Our separate actions object avoids the issue, at the cost of a slightly different style.

Third, middleware. Zustand's middleware wraps the state creator rather than setState. You write `create(devtools(persist((set) => ({ ... }))))`. Each middleware receives the creator function and returns a new creator, so it can wrap `set`, and also change the initial state or add to the api. That's more powerful than our setState wrapper, since hydrating and wrapping are both done in one place. Ours needed that hydrate special case in chapter six. If we rebuilt statekit, I'd probably adopt that creator-wrapping style, and I want you to see that as a legitimate design improvement, not just a difference.

Fourth, React integration. Zustand's `create` returns a hook. Under the hood it uses `useSyncExternalStore`, the React API designed for external stores, with a selector so a component only re-renders when its slice changes. That's the same subscribe and getState contract we built, which is exactly why it fits. Ours has no React binding yet, but you could write one in about ten lines, `useStore(store, selector)`, calling useSyncExternalStore with store.subscribe and a function that returns selector of getState. Selectors give you the fine-grained updates we talked about with prev state comparison.

Fifth, reactivity. Zustand has no Proxy tracking and no computed values built in. It deliberately stays with explicit selectors. We added computed, with dependency tracking, which is closer to Vue and Pinia, and that's actually a different philosophy rather than something missing. Choose explicit and simple, or automatic and magical. And finally, the unglamorous stuff. Zustand has years of edge cases handled: SSR hydration, devtools features, TypeScript types, extensive tests. Ours doesn't, and that's the honest gap. Next lecture, we publish what we have as an npm package. Pause here and think about which of those differences you would keep if you rebuilt the library tomorrow.

Let's publish statekit. Publishing sounds intimidating, but it's mostly a package.json with the right fields and a handful of terminal commands. First, I'll add one more file, src/index.js, that re-exports everything. `export { createStore } from './store.js'; export { reactive } from './reactive.js'; export { computed, effect } from './computed.js'; export { logger } from './logger.js'; export { persist } from './persist.js'; export { withHistory } from './history.js'; export { devtools } from './devtools.js';`. This is the public API. Anything not exported here is internal, and users can't depend on it, which gives you freedom to refactor later.

Now package.json. Run `npm init`, and answer the questions, or edit it by hand. The important fields: `name`, which must be unique on the registry, so check by searching npm, and if statekit is taken, use a scoped name like `@yourname/statekit`. `version`, starting at `0.1.0`. `type`: `module`, since we wrote ES modules. `main` and `exports`, which tell Node and bundlers which file to load, I'll set `exports` to `{ '.': './src/index.js' }`. And `files`: `['src']`, an allowlist so we publish only the source, not our demo folder or notes.

Before publishing, look at what you're about to ship. `npm pack --dry-run` lists every file that would go into the package tarball, with sizes. I always run this. It's how people discover they accidentally published a `.env` file or a two hundred megabyte folder. Ours should show package.json, README, and the seven or eight files in src. Speaking of README, write one. It's the first thing a stranger sees, and it should show the five line quickstart: import createStore, define state, add an action, subscribe, call the action. Also add a `license` field, like MIT, so people know they can use it.

Versioning follows semver, three numbers: major, minor, patch. Patch for bug fixes, minor for backward compatible features, major for breaking changes. Starting at zero point one means we're signalling that the API may still change. The command `npm version patch` bumps the number and creates a git tag in one step. Then, create an account on npmjs.com if you don't have one, run `npm login`, and finally `npm publish`. For scoped packages the first publish needs `npm publish --access public`, because scoped packages default to private. And turn on two factor authentication for your account, since a stolen npm token can poison everyone downstream.

There's a helper called np that I like. It's a package that wraps the whole release flow: it checks you're on the main branch with a clean working tree, runs your tests, bumps the version, publishes, and pushes the git tag, all interactively. You run `npx np` and follow the prompts. After publishing, test it like a user would. In an empty folder, `npm install statekit`, then import it in a small file and create a store. If that works, you've shipped a library. One last warning: you can unpublish only within a short window, so treat publish as permanent, and double check the dry run.

A word on trust. Real libraries also publish a built, minified bundle and type definitions so TypeScript users get autocomplete. You can write a `.d.ts` file by hand for a small library like ours, and point to it with the `types` field in package.json. Tools like tsup or Rollup produce the CommonJS and ESM bundles from the same source. We skipped that on purpose, since our code runs untouched in modern environments, but know it's the next step if you want broad compatibility. Alright. In the final lecture, a wrap up, and where you can go from here.

We made it. Let's take a minute to look at what you built. You started in lecture one with a plain object that couldn't tell anyone when it changed. Now you have statekit: a Proxy-based reactive primitive, a closure-based store with getState, setState, and subscribe, computed values with automatic dependency tracking and lazy caching, named actions with optimistic updates and rollback, a middleware chain with a logger and a persistence plugin, and a history system with undo, redo, and a bridge to Redux DevTools. All in plain JavaScript, a few hundred lines, and you understand every one of them.

More important than the code is what it changes about how you read other people's. When you open the Zustand source, you'll see the closure and the Set of listeners. In Redux Toolkit, you'll recognize the immutable updates and the middleware chain. In Pinia and Vue, you'll know the get trap tracks and the set trap triggers. These libraries stop being magic. They're variations on the same four or five ideas, with different tradeoffs. That's the real skill: when someone asks which state library to use, you can reason about it from first principles, instead of from hype.

If you'd like to keep going, here are some ideas, roughly in order of difficulty. Write the React binding, `useStore`, using `useSyncExternalStore` and a selector. Add batching, so multiple writes in one tick notify listeners only once, with a microtask. Fix the dependency cleanup in computed so stale dependencies get dropped on each run. Add a `subscribeWithSelector` helper that calls your listener only when a chosen slice changes. And grouped history entries, so a burst of changes undoes as one step. Each of these is a real feature in production libraries, and you now have the tools for all of them.

Beyond our library, here are things worth reading. The Vue reactivity documentation and source, particularly the effect and track functions, now that you've built a smaller version. Zustand's source, which you can read in an afternoon. The Redux documentation on immutability and middleware. And Immer, which does what our mutate idea did, but properly, with copy on write proxies. Then try building something with your library, maybe a drawing app, where undo matters, or a form wizard where persistence matters. Real use will show you the rough edges, and fixing those is how you learn.

Thank you for building this with me. A few practical reminders. Keep the statekit repository, put it on GitHub, and write that README, since a project you can show beats a project you can only describe. If you published it to npm, great, and if not, you still own the code. And do rebuild it from scratch in a week without looking, because that's when the understanding really sticks. I hope the next time you type `create` or `useStore`, you smile, knowing what's inside. Take care, and keep building. And again, thank you, truly, for sticking with it through all twenty four lectures, and I hope to see what you build next with it.
